title: Gradient-Based Learning Applied to Document Recognition (LeCun, Bottou, Bengio, Haffner, 1998)
excerpt: Convolutional Networks combine three architectural ideas to ensure some degree of shift, scale, and distortion invariance: local receptive fields, shared weights (or weight replication), and spatial or temporal sub-sampling. ... Each unit in a layer receives inputs from a set of units located in a small neighborhood in the previous layer. ... Units in a layer are organized in planes within which all the units share the same set of weights. The set of outputs of the units in such a plane is called a feature map. Units in a feature map are all constrained to perform the same operation on different parts of the image. ... the unit computes a weighted sum of its inputs within its receptive field, adds a trainable bias, and passes the result through a squashing function. ... Once a feature has been detected, its exact location becomes less important. Only its approximate position relative to other features is relevant. ... A simple way to reduce the precision with which the position of distinctive features are encoded in a feature map is to reduce the spatial resolution of the feature map. This can be achieved with a so-called sub-sampling layer which performs a local averaging and a sub-sampling.
focus: Explain a single 2-D convolution feature map with shared weights on a small 6x6 binary image and an editable 3x3 kernel (stride 1, no padding), followed by 2x2 average sub-sampling. Let the learner edit the kernel and bias and select the input pattern. Show the sliding receptive field, each weighted sum, the 4x4 feature map and the 2x2 pooled map. Check that shifting the input pattern by one pixel shifts the feature map by one position, and that the output size is (6-3+1). Explain why shared weights detect the same feature anywhere. Do not train the network.
audience: Engineering undergraduate who knows matrices and sums but not neural networks.
